did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a threefold call to sing to the LORD, emphasizing that the call is addressed to “all the earth”—not just to a particular group.
The verse connects singing, blessing the LORD’s name, and proclaiming his salvation day by day, presenting worship of the LORD as an ongoing practice.
The singers are called to tell the nations about the LORD’s glory and proclaim his wonders among all peoples; thus, the chapter emphasizes a witness addressed to the entire world.
The LORD’s greatness is described through several expressions: he is great, greatly praised, and to be feared above all gods.
The chapter contrasts the gods of the nations, described as idols, with the LORD, of whom it says: “He made the heavens.”
The phrase “families of the nations” extends the call to worship the LORD to all peoples, not merely to individuals or to one nation.

This verse contains three declarations about the LORD’s reign: the LORD reigns, the world is firmly established and cannot be moved, and he judges the peoples with fairness—that is, with upright and just judgment.
The joy of the LORD’s reign is portrayed as the joy of all creation: the heavens, the earth, the sea, and everything in it all respond to the manifestation of his kingship.
The fields and the trees of the forest are also described as rejoicing and singing for joy, poetically presenting creation as a participant in praise.

The conclusion explains the reason for this joy: the LORD comes to judge the earth, to judge the world in righteousness and the peoples in his faithfulness; judgment is portrayed as part of his reign, not its opposite.
